name: Nora Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, with a vocational certificate, and I've run the pressure cooker for sealed cans at this food plant for years. The plant calls it a retort. I check the temperature chart, load the rack and make sure a batch is cool before anyone opens the door. I know the routine, though a stubborn valve still sends me for the fitter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are home and new technology like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a part-time school caretaker, and our grown children have moved away. We rent, my operator pay is low, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. Only a few canneries are close enough for the bus trip. I use AI every day to sort errands and translate a recipe, but I check its answers. I would like to stop at 69 in 2037 if documented income then covers rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the canning crew that a quiet AI future still leaves someone checking the temperature chart. A can that misses its proper heat cycle is not made safe by a neat computer label. I would welcome a faster office schedule if the factory keeps paying the operators who make the food safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work itself looks steady, but our rent and my partner's part-time caretaker pay leave almost no cushion. I am experienced on the retort; that does not raise my wage. If the machine needs a major repair, I worry that shifts could be cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking each canning batch's chart before the rack comes out and write down valve faults for the fitter. I'll put a small amount from each full-pay week into a fresh emergency pot after rent. If an AI-assisted temperature log is approved, I will learn its alert controls on a paid shift and compare them with the paper chart before relying on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary household money, even with no big AI change. A full canning chart cannot fill an empty rent envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you hold a canning batch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sudden flat line on the chart could mean the sensor has failed or the heat stopped. I hold the rack and call the fitter; I do not wave the batch through. The paper record stays beside the machine until the fault is resolved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How steady are the caretaker hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's school caretaker hours are part-time, and some weeks include fewer shifts. We pay rent from the wages that actually arrive. A small new deposit after a full week is possible, but existing cash cannot stretch itself.

say: **Temperature charts** still need an experienced retort operator.
Faster scheduling should preserve **paid canning shifts** and safe food.
think: Our **thin reserve** and part-time caretaker income make rent tight already.
A major **retort repair** could cancel paid shifts despite my experience.
do: **Check** batch charts and log valve faults for the fitter.
**Save** new money from full weeks after rent and learn approved AI alerts against the paper chart.
feel: **Anxious** about current household income even without major AI change.
S0.quote: A full canning chart cannot fill an empty rent envelope.
fieldNote: She has **vocational training and experience** on the retort, yet low pay and under a month saved.
Her **fresh deposits** come from full wages; learning AI alert controls requires an approved log and paid practice against paper.

steps.text: Keep checking canning batch charts and recording valve faults
Save new wages from full weeks after rent
Learn approved AI alert controls against paper chart on paid shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could set orders and write batch paperwork before any robot lifts the racks. I would try an approved alarm log if it actually catches faults, but the fitter and I still have to make the retort safe. Management should show us what hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Canning is physical, but a smarter schedule could combine batches and remove my paid setup hours. With less than a month saved, even a small cut would hit rent. I can learn a useful new display quickly if I am allowed to practise on a real paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor for the posted setup rota and compare it with four pay slips. If the plant offers a funded paid guarded course on the alarm log, I'll enrol and use it with the fitter on an actual stopped retort. I'll ask about any missing setup hours before I count a promised busy season as pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I am curious about an alarm that works, but a shorter rota would reach our household first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the new alarm log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to see the log flag a known temperature dip and then find that dip on the paper chart. I would learn the controls with the fitter beside a stopped machine. An AI summary at home is no proof that a batch is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which hours would show a real cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The setup line on the rota tells me whether I still get paid for loading and testing each batch. I would compare it with the last four pay slips and ask the supervisor about an actual gap. A plan for more cans later cannot pay this month's rent.

say: **Order AI** may change batch schedules before robots handle can racks.
A useful alarm needs **paid hands-on practice** and a real safety check.
think: Combined batches could cut **setup hours** and threaten rent quickly.
I can learn an **approved alarm log**, but it must match the paper chart.
do: **Compare** the posted setup rota with pay slips.
**Enrol** in funded paid guarded log training if offered and practise with the fitter on a stopped retort.
feel: **Anxious** about paid setup hours while curious about useful alarms.
S1.quote: A plan for more cans later cannot pay this month's rent.
fieldNote: The direct risk is **paid setup time**, while physical rack handling remains exposed later to robots.
Actual **log training** requires an offered funded paid guarded place; comparing rosters is evidence gathering, not a guaranteed recovery.

steps.text: Compare posted canning setup rota with four pay slips
Enrol in alarm-log course if funded paid guarded place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI could plan the canning runs by 2028 and robots might lift the racks around 2031, when I am 63. That is far before my hoped-for stop at 69. I want the plant to tell us which operators still have paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my retort shifts to go if robots can load, run and unload the racks. We have less than a month saved and only a few canneries nearby. I was awake after two shifts were cancelled last winter; losing the line would leave me lying there again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a written shift plan and a funded paid guarded place in can-quality inspection. If it is actually offered, I'll enrol and practise with the fitter on rejected batches. If my retort hours go, I'll apply to posted safe local food-packing work only if the wage after bus fare covers rent; after qualifying, I'll also apply to posted can-inspection work on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I could lose the wage at 63 and have years to pay for before an affordable stop. A robot may lift the can rack, but it will not lift our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must can-inspection training cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course must show me a swollen can, a bad heat record and when to hold a whole lot. I need supervised practice on paid time, with fees covered and the rack guarded. I cannot buy tuition with our rent reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another job affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a real local posting with safe hours, a base wage and a bus route. The amount left after travel must cover rent and food with my partner's actual caretaker pay. An inspection post would also require the completed practical qualification.

say: **2031 robots** could take retort shifts when I am 63.
The plant should give operators **written paid-work plans** before changing racks.
think: I expect a **major loss** of retort wages.
Our **thin reserve** and few nearby canneries cannot bridge six years to a hoped-for stop.
do: **Request** written shifts and a funded paid guarded inspection place.
**Apply** to posted safe local packing or qualified can inspection if displaced and net pay covers rent.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected lost wages and remembered sleeplessness after cancelled shifts.
S2.quote: A robot may lift the can rack, but it will not lift our rent.
fieldNote: Her **expected major shift loss** and prior lost sleep support alarm despite willingness to learn.
Both **job applications** need real safe local postings and rent-covering net pay; inspection also needs funded paid guarded qualification.

steps.text: Enrol in can inspection if funded paid guarded fitter-led place offered
Apply to posted safe local packing if displaced and net pay covers rent
Apply to posted safe local can inspection if qualified, displaced, net pay covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could set the orders by 2031, while capable robots reach the retort around 2034, when I am 66. Three more paid years would help us save and learn inspection. I still need income after 66 unless the household numbers change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our small reserve will not fund retirement just because I am near 70. My partner's part-time pay is not enough for rent alone. I could make use of the warning if the plant actually pays for safe inspection practice and there is a local opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll put a little from each full-pay week into our reserve after rent. If the plant offers a funded paid guarded inspection place, I'll complete it with the fitter. If retort hours fall after I qualify, I'll apply for posted safe local can-inspection work only if net pay after travel covers our costs; without a course place, I'll look for posted safe local packing on the same pay terms if displaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the later date still comes before I can assume retirement is affordable. At least there is time to seek a real place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an inspection practical test prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have to find a can with a broken seal and match it to the heat record before releasing a lot. The fitter should watch the stop and check my decision on paid time. A can-inspection brochure would not make me qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would packing be your fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A packing opening would need a safe local site and a wage that covers rent after the bus fare. I would use that fallback only if there is no offered inspection place and my retort hours go. I won't confuse a vacancy advert with a signed wage.

say: **2031 order AI** gives time before retort robots around 2034.
Paid inspection practice and a **real local opening** would make that time useful.
think: At **66**, part-time caretaker pay and a small reserve may not cover rent.
A **funded course place** matters only if it leads to qualified paid work.
do: **Save** fresh full-week wages after rent and attend offered funded paid guarded inspection.
**Apply** to posted safe local inspection if qualified and hours fall, or packing if no course is offered.
feel: **Anxious** about income before an affordable retirement.
S3.quote: A can-inspection brochure would not make me qualified.
fieldNote: The **inspection application** requires an actual funded paid guarded place, completed qualification and viable posted local net pay.
The **packing fallback** has its own no-course and lost-hours trigger; she does not add that trigger to the qualified inspection path.

steps.text: Save new full-week canning wages after rent
Attend can inspection if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours fall, net pay sufficient
Apply to posted safe local packing if no course, displaced, net pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children that thinking AI may plan cans in 2036 when I am 68, and robots might run the racks around 2039 when I am 71. I hope to stop at 69 in 2037. A whole decade helps only if we use the paid years and check what income comes after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have almost no reserve now. Even with a long warning, I cannot assume a pension amount or that my partner will get more caretaker hours. If documented post-work income covers rent and food at 69, I can stop in 2037; otherwise I may still need a paid retort or packing shift when robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will list rent and food, request written figures for income after I stop, and compare them before promising 2037. I'll keep the retort shift and save new money from full-pay weeks. If the figures cover bills, I'll stop at 69 in 2037; if I am still working after 2036 and hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local food work only where net pay after travel covers our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about how little we have saved, though the time gives me ways to act. A decade of warning will not replace a missing retort wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figures could support a 2037 exit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need the actual monthly amount available after my work ends and the bills that remain. Part-time caretaker hours should be counted at what my partner earns, not a wished-for full week. If the numbers do not cover rent, I will not hand in notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you seek later factory work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for a real food-plant posting with safe shifts and a base wage that works after bus fare. I would only apply if I was still employed and my paid hours had fallen. If I have stopped with enough income in 2037, I won't be job hunting at 71.

say: **2036 order AI** and later robots allow time to check income.
I hope to **stop in 2037** only if documented money pays rent and food.
think: Our **thin reserve** and part-time second wage cannot guarantee retirement.
If income is short at **69**, I may still need a paid shift after 2037.
do: **Compare** written post-work income with bills and stop at 69 only if affordable.
**Keep** earning and saving; apply later only if still employed, hours fall and local net pay works.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings despite the longer warning.
S4.quote: A decade of warning will not replace a missing retort wage.
fieldNote: The **2037 stop** is conditional on documented income against costs, with no assumed pension or benefit entitlement.
The **post-2036 job search** requires continued employment, lost hours and an actual safe local post with rent-covering net pay.

steps.text: Compare documented post-work income with rent and food
Save new full-week retort wages after rent
Stop retort shift at 69 in 2037 if documented income covers bills
Apply to posted safe local food if employed after 2036, hours fall, net pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case. Robot racks around 2031 could end my retort wage at 63, long before we have money to stop. I need written shifts, a funded paid guarded inspection place and actual safe local postings with enough pay after the bus fare. A household income calculation must decide whether 2037 is possible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the heat chart when a machine says a canning batch is fine. A sealed food can looks ordinary even when its heat record is wrong.

headlineQuote: A sealed food can looks ordinary even when its heat record is wrong.
portrait: **Nora**, 58, is an experienced canning-retort operator with a vocational certificate and daily checked AI use.
She and her part-time school-caretaker partner have **grown children**, low operator pay, under a month saved and few nearby canneries.
Her **centrist outlook** asks for written hours and workable training; she tries new tools early but tests them against physical batch records.
She is **alarmed** by expected fast retort-wage loss; stopping at 69 depends on documented household income covering rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring rack-handling robots around 2031 and end retort pay at 63.
whatWouldHelp: **Written shifts**, funded paid guarded inspection and actual safe local roles with rent-covering net pay would help.
